groups.title: Seniority & Career Level
groups.finding: Your profile reads as Junior/early-career for this target role: 6.4 years of work history is in retail (Bunnings, Coles), with 0 relevant years in clinical/lab employment. Your Biomedical Science degree is a strong foundation, but your own cover letter also states you do not yet have lab experience outside university.
examples: "I don't have any lab experience outside of uni."
6.4 total years in retail roles, 0 relevant years to Laboratory Technician (Biochemistry)
groups.recommendation: Confirm Junior (graduate-entry) framing and present yourself as a capable new starter: emphasise degree-based lab foundations, procedural discipline, and readiness for structured training rather than over-claiming direct lab experience.
groups.insight: Correct seniority framing prevents credibility loss and helps recruiters assess you against the right benchmark for a Grade 1 role.

recommended_overrides.seniority_level: Junior (0 relevant / 6.4 total yrs — confirmed by user)
recommended_overrides.positioning_strategy: Use graduate-entry positioning: foundational technical knowledge + high reliability + strong trainability.
recommended_overrides.claim_calibration: Avoid implied claims of prior clinical lab practice; frame university practical exposure clearly and honestly.

groups.title: Formatting & Bullet Style
groups.finding: Your CV bullets are mostly short gerund fragments and bare phrases (e.g., "Helping customers find products", "Garden section mostly") rather than standard action-result bullet writing. Several lines also use casual spoken wording (e.g., "sometimes worked in the deli when they needed people").
examples: "sometimes worked in the deli when they needed people"
groups.recommendation: Rewrite bullets with past-tense action verbs and clearer task context (what you did, where, and to what standard). Keep the concise length, but upgrade from shorthand fragments to professional achievement-oriented bullets.
groups.insight: Recruiters read bullet form as a proxy for workplace communication quality; professional structure improves trust immediately.

recommended_overrides.bullet_verb_style: Start work-history bullets with past-tense action verbs (e.g., Assisted, Managed, Coordinated).
recommended_overrides.bullet_clarity: Replace bare noun/gerund fragments with complete role-relevant statements containing task + context.
recommended_overrides.register_control: Remove conversational wording and use formal professional phrasing throughout CV bullets.

groups.title: Linguistic Strength
groups.finding: Language choices currently weaken perceived professionalism: the skills list is dominated by low-value clichés ("Team player", "Reliable", "Good at following instructions") and there is no quantified evidence to support claims. Overall voice is mixed/casual rather than evidence-led.
groups.recommendation: Replace generic trait words with specific, evidence-backed statements tied to responsibilities, consistency, accuracy, or process compliance. Prioritise concrete transferable signals over personal adjectives.
groups.insight: Evidence-based language carries far more screening value than self-descriptors, especially when transitioning industries.

recommended_overrides.evidence_first_language: Convert generic soft-skill claims into concrete, task-linked statements with context.
recommended_overrides.cliche_removal: Remove unsupported clichés from the skills section and replace with role-relevant capabilities.
recommended_overrides.quantification_prompt: Add numbers where available (tenure, shift volume, transaction accuracy context) to strengthen credibility.

groups.title: Cover Letter Style
groups.finding: Your cover letter tone is currently self-undermining and too informal for healthcare hiring. It opens with self-deprecation ("I know I probably don't have as much experience...") and includes personal remarks like "I never call in sick unless I actually am", which can read as defensive rather than professional.
examples: "I know I probably don't have as much experience as other people applying..."
"I never call in sick unless I actually am"
groups.recommendation: Shift to confident, factual framing: start with your degree and lab-ready fundamentals, then connect transferable reliability and willingness to train to the Grade 1 pathway. Remove apologetic or personal-defensive lines.
groups.insight: Cover letter opening tone strongly shapes first impression; confidence plus accuracy improves interview probability.

recommended_overrides.opening_frame: Open with qualification-fit and role motivation, not comparative self-doubt.
recommended_overrides.tone_policy: Use formal, confident, evidence-led language; remove apologetic and overly personal statements.
recommended_overrides.transferable_bridge: Bridge retail experience to lab context through reliability, procedural consistency, and attention to detail.

groups.title: Professional Presentation Signals
groups.finding: Two presentation details may create avoidable friction at first glance: a casual legacy email handle (sarahj_2001@hotmail.com) and listing an expired First Aid certificate (expired 2022).
groups.recommendation: Use a cleaner professional email format and remove expired credentials until renewed. Keep credentials current and date-valid when listed.
groups.insight: Small credibility cues can influence early screening outcomes before your core experience is fully read.

recommended_overrides.contact_professionalism: Use a professional email format (e.g., firstname.lastname domain) in CV header.
recommended_overrides.credential_validity: Do not list expired certificates; re-add only once renewed with current validity dates.

groups.title: Professional Summary — Voice
groups.finding: Your professional summary can be written in first person (you speaking as yourself) or third person (written about you).
examples: First person: "Biomedical Science graduate with hands-on laboratory training…"
Third person: "Sarah is a Biomedical Science graduate with hands-on laboratory training…"
groups.recommendation: Use first person — it reads as direct and modern and is the most common choice today. Prefer third person? Pick "Customise" and type "third person".
groups.insight: First person (or implied first person, with no "I") is standard for most professional summaries; third person can suit very senior or academic profiles.

recommended_overrides.profile_voice: first person — the summary speaks as the candidate (implied first person, no name and no third-person pronouns)
